g10-physics-up6-t1.overview: Light is an electromagnetic wave — oscillating electric and magnetic fields racing through space at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Visible light is just a sliver of a vast family: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma, all the same phenomenon at different frequencies.
objectives: Describe the nature and properties of electromagnetic waves
Use c = fλ for any EM wave
Order the EM spectrum by frequency, wavelength and energy
Match each band to its production, uses and hazards
g10-physics-up6-t1.simple: Shake an electric charge and you send out a wave — that's an electromagnetic (EM) wave. All EM waves travel at light-speed in vacuum and need no medium (sunlight crosses empty space). The only difference between a radio wave and a gamma ray is frequency: radio = lazy, long waves; gamma = frantic, tiny waves. Higher frequency = more energy = more dangerous to your cells.
g10-physics-up6-t1.detailed:
Nature of EM waves: mutually perpendicular oscillating electric and magnetic fields, perpendicular to the direction of travel — so EM waves are transverse. They can be reflected, refracted, diffracted and polarised, and travel through vacuum at c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s.

The wave equation: c = fλ, where f is frequency (Hz) and λ wavelength (m). Since c is fixed in vacuum, high frequency ⇒ short wavelength.

The spectrum (increasing f, decreasing λ, increasing photon energy):
• Radio — broadcasting, communications; metres to km.
• Microwave — ovens (2.45 GHz heats water), Wi-Fi, radar, satellite links.
• Infrared — 'heat radiation': remote controls, thermal cameras, night vision.
• Visible — red (long, ~700 nm) to violet (short, ~400 nm); the only band our eyes detect.
• Ultraviolet — sterilising, fluorescent lamps, vitamin D; causes sunburn, skin cancer (ionising at the high end).
• X-rays — medical imaging, security scanners; penetrate soft tissue, stopped by bone/lead; ionising.
• Gamma rays — radioactive nuclei, cancer radiotherapy, sterilising food; most penetrating, most dangerous.

Common misconception: the bands differ only in frequency/wavelength — the wave itself is identical in nature. There is no sharp boundary between adjacent bands.

Ionising vs non-ionising: UV/X/gamma photons carry enough energy to knock electrons off atoms (ionisation) → DNA damage → cancer risk. Radio→visible don't (they mainly heat).

keyTerms.def: Transverse wave of oscillating electric and magnetic fields; travels at c in vacuum.
Wave equation for EM radiation in vacuum.
The full range of EM waves ordered by frequency/wavelength.
EM radiation energetic enough to remove electrons from atoms (UV high end, X, γ).
Oscillations perpendicular to travel direction — proven for light by polarisation.

formulas.name: Wave equation for light
formulas.meaning: Speed of light equals frequency times wavelength.
formulas.when: Any EM wave in vacuum/air: find the missing one of c, f, λ.

workedExamples.problem: A Wi-Fi router transmits at 2.4 GHz. Find the wavelength.
workedExamples.answer: About 12.5 cm — comparable to the size of a room, which is why Wi-Fi diffracts around furniture.

workedExamples.problem: Green light has wavelength 500 nm. Find its frequency. (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m)
workedExamples.answer: 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz — hundreds of trillions of oscillations per second.

commonMistakes: Thinking microwaves, infrared and X-rays are fundamentally different 'kinds' of stuff — they're all EM waves, differing only in f and λ.
Believing EM waves need a medium (they don't — sound does, light doesn't).
Mixing up the order: gamma has the HIGHEST frequency, radio the LOWEST.
Forgetting to convert GHz → Hz and nm → m before using c = fλ.
applications: Radio/TV broadcasting, mobile phones, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth — the communications backbone.
Microwave ovens, radar speed guns, satellite navigation.
Infrared remotes, thermal imaging (electrical faults, fever screening), night vision.
UV sterilisation of water and surgical tools; fluorescence in security inks.
X-ray imaging and CT; gamma radiotherapy (e.g. cobalt-60) and food sterilisation.
g10-physics-up6-t1.summary: All EM waves: transverse, travel at c = 3×10⁸ m/s in vacuum, obey c = fλ. Spectrum from radio (long λ, low f) to gamma (short λ, high f). Higher f ⇒ more energy ⇒ ionising danger (UV/X/γ). Same wave, different frequency.

g10-physics-up6-t2.overview: Light bounces off surfaces (reflection) and bends when it changes medium (refraction). Two precise laws — angle in = angle out, and Snell's law — let you predict mirrors, straws-in-water, and why pools look shallow.
objectives: State and apply the two laws of reflection
Explain refraction and why light bends at a boundary
Use Snell's law and n = c/v, and define refractive index
g10-physics-up6-t2.simple: Reflection: the angle light hits a mirror equals the angle it leaves — measured from the NORMAL (the perpendicular line), not the surface. Refraction: light slows down entering glass or water, and if it arrives at an angle, one side of the wavefront slows first — the ray bends. Into denser (slower): bends TOWARD the normal. Out: bends AWAY. That bending is why a straw looks broken in a glass.
g10-physics-up6-t2.detailed:
Laws of reflection: (1) The incident ray, reflected ray and normal all lie in one plane. (2) Angle of incidence = angle of reflection (θᵢ = θᵣ), always measured from the normal.

Regular vs diffuse: a smooth surface (mirror) reflects parallel rays parallel → clear image. A rough surface scatters rays in all directions (diffuse) → you see the surface itself from any angle, but no reflection of the source. Both obey the laws — microscopic bumps just point the normals every which way.

Refraction: light changes speed between media. The refractive index n = c/v (always ≥ 1; vacuum n = 1, air ≈ 1.0003, water 1.33, glass ≈ 1.5, diamond 2.42). Bigger n = slower light = 'optically denser'.

Snell's law: n₁ sinθ₁ = n₂ sinθ₂ (angles from the normal). Entering a higher-n medium → bends toward the normal; lower n → away.

Special cases:
• Normal incidence (θ = 0): slows down but does NOT bend.
• Total internal reflection: travelling toward a LOWER-n medium past the critical angle c (where sin c = n₂/n₁), no refracted ray exists — all light reflects. This runs optical fibres and sparkling diamonds.

Consequences: apparent depth < real depth (pool looks shallow); objects appear displaced; prisms split white light because n varies slightly with colour (dispersion); mirages come from gradual refraction in hot air layers.

keyTerms.def: Line perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence — angles are measured from it.
n = c/v, how much a medium slows light.
n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂ governing bending at a boundary.
Incidence angle (in the denser medium) beyond which refraction vanishes.
Complete reflection when light tries to exit a denser medium past the critical angle.
Scattering of light from a rough surface in many directions.

formulas.name: Critical angle
formulas.meaning: The angle where the refracted ray grazes the surface (θ₂ = 90°).

workedExamples.problem: A ray in air strikes water (n = 1.33) at 40° to the normal. Find the angle of refraction.
workedExamples.answer: ≈ 29° — bent toward the normal, as expected entering a denser medium.

workedExamples.problem: Light travels at 2.0 × 10⁸ m/s in a glass block. Find its refractive index, and the critical angle for glass→air.

commonMistakes: Measuring angles from the SURFACE instead of the normal (a 30° 'grazing' ray is actually 60° incidence).
Bending the wrong way: into denser → toward the normal.
Forgetting total internal reflection needs BOTH: going to a lower-n medium AND exceeding the critical angle.
Thinking the reflected ray disappears in refraction — usually partial reflection always happens too.
applications: Optical fibres: light bounces by total internal reflection carrying internet/phone data.
Endoscopes let doctors see inside the body using fibre bundles.
Prisms in binoculars/periscopes use TIR instead of mirrors (no tarnish, 100% efficient).
Lenses in glasses, cameras, microscopes — all designed with Snell's law.
Diamonds sparkle because n = 2.42 gives a tiny 24° critical angle — light traps inside.
g10-physics-up6-t2.summary: Reflection: θᵢ = θᵣ from the normal. Refraction: light changes speed (n = c/v) and bends per Snell n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂ — toward normal entering denser. Past the critical angle (sin c = n₂/n₁), total internal reflection — the trick behind fibres and sparkles.

steps: Beyond critical angle → total internal reflection

g10-physics-up6-t3.overview: Curved mirrors and lenses form images by reflection and refraction. With a few ray rules and one equation, you can predict every image — real or virtual, upright or inverted, magnified or diminished — from torch reflectors to camera lenses.
objectives: Construct ray diagrams for concave and convex mirrors
Describe image properties for each object position
Construct ray diagrams for converging and diverging lenses
Use the mirror/lens equation and magnification formula
g10-physics-up6-t3.simple: Concave mirror (caves in): focuses light to a real point — makeup mirrors magnify your face, torches throw a parallel beam. Convex mirror (bulges out): always gives a smaller upright wide view — car wing mirrors ('objects closer than they appear'). Convex lens: same job as concave mirror but by refraction; concave lens always shrinks and spreads. One equation handles them all: 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, with m = v/u for size.
g10-physics-up6-t3.detailed:
Setup: principal axis through the centre of curvature C and pole/centre; focal point F halfway from pole to C (f = R/2). Object distance u, image distance v, focal length f.

Three rays you need (any two locate the image):
1. Parallel to axis → reflects/refracts through F.
2. Through F → leaves parallel to axis.
3. Through the centre (C for mirrors, optical centre for lenses) → undeviated.

Concave mirror image table (object distance u vs f, R = 2f):
• u > 2f: real, inverted, diminished, between F and C (used: nothing special — general imaging).
• u = 2f: real, inverted, SAME size at C.
• f < u < 2f: real, inverted, magnified beyond C (projectors).
• u = f: no image (rays parallel — torches/spotlights send parallel beams this way).
• u < f: virtual, upright, magnified behind mirror (shaving/makeup mirrors).

Convex mirror: ALWAYS virtual, upright, diminished, behind the mirror — wide field of view (shop security, wing mirrors).

Converging (convex) lens: same table as the concave mirror (real images when u > f; magnifying glass when u < f). Diverging (concave) lens: always virtual, upright, diminished.

Equations (real-is-positive convention): 1/f = 1/u + 1/v; magnification m = v/u (image height/object height). Virtual image ⇒ v negative; diverging devices ⇒ f negative.

Real vs virtual: real images form where rays actually meet — can be projected on a screen, always inverted. Virtual images form where rays only appear to come from — cannot be screened, upright.

keyTerms.def: Point where rays parallel to the axis converge (or appear to diverge from).
Distance from pole/optical centre to F; f = R/2 for spherical mirrors.
Formed by actual ray intersection; projectable; inverted.
Formed by apparent ray divergence; not projectable; upright.
m = v/u = image height / object height.
Thicker in the middle (convex); brings parallel rays to a focus.

formulas.name: Magnification
formulas.meaning: Image size relative to object size.
formulas.when: To find image size or whether it's enlarged.
formulas.example: v = 30, u = 15 → m = 2: image twice the object's size.

workedExamples.problem: A concave mirror has f = 10 cm. An object 4 cm tall stands 30 cm away. Find the image position, size and nature.
workedExamples.given: f = 10 cm, u = 30 cm, h = 4 cm
workedExamples.answer: Image 15 cm in front of the mirror, 2 cm tall, real and inverted (u > 2f case).

workedExamples.problem: A lens of focal length 20 cm must project a sharp image of a slide onto a screen 80 cm away. Where should the slide go?
workedExamples.given: f = +20 cm (converging), v = 80 cm (real image on screen)
workedExamples.answer: Place the slide ≈ 26.7 cm from the lens; the image is 3× magnified, inverted.

commonMistakes: Mixing up which mirror converges: CONCAVE mirrors converge (like a convex lens); mnemonics: 'cave catches light'.
Forgetting f = R/2 — the focus is halfway to the centre of curvature.
Sign errors: virtual image ⇒ v negative; diverging lens/convex mirror ⇒ f negative.
Saying a magnifying glass makes a real image — held close (u < f) it makes a virtual, upright, magnified one.
Measuring u and v from the wrong point (always from the pole/optical centre).
applications: Car headlight and torch reflectors: bulb at F sends a parallel beam out.
Makeup/shaving mirrors: concave with face inside f → magnified upright face.
Rear-view wing mirrors & shop security: convex → wide view, diminished image.
Cameras and projectors: converging lenses form real images on film/sensor/screen.
Microscopes and telescopes: combinations of lenses multiply magnification.
Corrective glasses: converging lenses for long-sightedness, diverging for short-sightedness.
g10-physics-up6-t3.summary: Three standard rays locate any image. Concave mirrors/converging lenses: real inverted images outside f, virtual magnified inside f. Convex mirrors/diverging lenses: always virtual, upright, diminished. 1/f = 1/u + 1/v, m = v/u, f = R/2.

steps: Draw ray parallel to axis → through F
Draw ray through F → leaves parallel

g10-physics-up6-t4.overview: Your eye is a living camera: a lens focuses light onto a film of millions of detectors. And colour is not painted onto objects — it's the light they choose to reflect. This topic ties the whole optics unit to real life: glasses, rainbows and why the sky is blue.
objectives: Describe the structure of the eye and how it focuses (accommodation)
Explain short- and long-sightedness and their lens corrections
Explain the dispersion of white light and the colour spectrum
Describe additive (primary) and subtractive (pigment) colour mixing
g10-physics-up6-t4.simple: Light enters the cornea and pupil (the iris's adjustable hole), the lens flexes to focus on a retina full of light sensors, and the brain flips the inverted image. Young lenses squeeze to see close — that ability (accommodation) fades with age. Colour: a red shirt isn't red-painted — it absorbs every colour except red, which it bounces to you. Mix coloured LIGHT and red+green+blue = white; mix PAINT and all colours ≈ black/brown.
g10-physics-up6-t4.detailed:
Eye structure & function:
• Cornea: does most of the bending (refraction) of incoming light.
• Iris: muscular diaphragm controlling the pupil size (large in dim light, small in bright).
• Accommodation: ciliary muscles change lens shape — thicker/stronger for near objects, thinner for far. The near point (~25 cm for a young adult) and far point (infinity for a normal eye) bound clear vision.
• Retina: the 'film' — rods (dim-light, monochrome, peripheral) and cones (colour, detail; concentrated in the fovea). Optic nerve carries signals to the brain; the blind spot is where the nerve exits (no receptors).
• The image on the retina is real, inverted and diminished — the brain interprets it upright.

Defects & correction:
• Myopia (short-sighted): eyeball too long / lens too strong → far images focus IN FRONT of the retina. Correct with a diverging (concave) lens.
• Hyperopia (long-sighted): eyeball too short / weak lens → near images focus BEHIND the retina. Correct with a converging (convex) lens.
• Presbyopia (ageing stiff lens), astigmatism (irregular cornea), cataract (clouded lens) round out the common conditions.

Colour & dispersion: white light is a mixture of all visible wavelengths. A prism refracts each colour differently (n is larger for violet) → violet bends most, red least → the spectrum ROYGBIV. Rainbows are dispersion + internal reflection in raindrops.

Additive mixing (lights): primaries Red, Green, Blue. R+G = yellow, R+B = magenta, G+B = cyan, R+G+B = white. (Screens use RGB pixels.)

Subtractive mixing (pigments/filters): primaries Cyan, Magenta, Yellow (school texts often say red, yellow, blue). Each pigment absorbs some colours and reflects the rest: a green leaf reflects green, absorbs red+blue. A red filter transmits only red. An object appears black if it absorbs everything, white if it reflects everything. Printer inks are CMY(K).

keyTerms.def: Changing lens shape to focus at different distances.
Closest distance of distinct vision (~25 cm young adult).
Short-sightedness: distant focus in front of the retina; concave lens corrects.
Long-sightedness: near focus behind the retina; convex lens corrects.
Splitting white light into colours because n depends on wavelength.
Red, green, blue lights — combine to white.
Cyan, magenta, yellow pigments — each removes (absorbs) colours.

workedExamples.problem: A student can see clearly only up to 2 m. Diagnose the defect and explain the correction.
workedExamples.formula: Myopia: image of distant objects forms in front of the retina.
workedExamples.substitution: A diverging lens spreads incoming parallel rays so the eye's lens can bring them onto the retina.
workedExamples.calculation: (Lens power: P = −1/2 = −0.5 D for distance vision.)
workedExamples.answer: Short-sightedness (myopia), corrected with a concave (diverging) lens.

workedExamples.problem: A white T-shirt is viewed through a red filter. What colour does it appear, and why?
workedExamples.given: White reflects all colours; red filter transmits only red.
workedExamples.formula: Subtractive filtering: only the transmitted colour reaches the eye.
workedExamples.substitution: The shirt reflects red light; the filter passes it.
workedExamples.calculation: No other colours exist to be blocked.
workedExamples.answer: The shirt appears RED — it reflects every colour, but only red gets through the filter.

workedExamples.problem: Why does a blue flower look black under pure yellow light?
workedExamples.given: Yellow light = red + green (additive). Blue pigment absorbs red and green, reflects blue.
workedExamples.formula: An object can only reflect colours that illuminate it.
workedExamples.substitution: No blue in the yellow light; the pigment absorbs the red and green components.
workedExamples.answer: The flower absorbs all the yellow light's components and has no blue to reflect — it appears black.

commonMistakes: Saying the lens does most of the refraction — the CORNEA does; the lens fine-tunes (accommodation).
Swapping the corrections: myopia → concave, hyperopia → convex.
Thinking objects 'contain' colour — they reflect some wavelengths and absorb the rest.
Confusing additive (RGB lights → white) with subtractive (pigments → dark) mixing.
Believing the retina image is upright — it's inverted; the brain flips perception.
applications: Glasses, contact lenses and LASER eye surgery all reshape focusing power.
Cameras copy the eye: aperture ≈ pupil, lens ≈ eye lens, sensor ≈ retina.
TVs/phones build every colour from RGB subpixels (additive mixing).
Colour printing uses CMYK inks (subtractive mixing).
Rainbows, prism spectroscopy and fibre-optic colour signals all come from dispersion.
Night-vision and astronomy exploit rod sensitivity; fovea detail explains why we point our eyes directly.
g10-physics-up6-t4.summary: Eye = cornea (main bend) + adjustable lens (accommodation) + retina (rods/cones) forming a real inverted image. Myopia → concave lens; hyperopia → convex. White light = all colours (dispersion proves it). Additive primaries RGB → white; pigments absorb (subtract) — objects only reflect the light they're given.
